Practicum Activity: EDA and Predictive Modeling on the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset

Practicum 1 - TOTD 2026/27

Your Team C - L1 / Oriol Arasa, Izan Flores, Andreu Jordà, Jordi Vivas

2026-10-14

1 Overview

In this practicum, you will work with the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset (Kaggle: uciml/pima-indians-diabetes-database) to practice the full data analysis pipeline: exploration, cleaning, visualization, and predictive modeling. The dataset contains diagnostic measurements for female patients of Pima Indian heritage, aged 21 and older, and a binary outcome indicating whether the patient has diabetes.

Estimated time: 2–3 hours Deliverable: This completed .Rmd file, knitted to HTML, with all code chunks filled in and all reflection questions answered in the text.

1.1 Learning Objectives

By the end of this activity, you should be able to:

  1. Load, inspect, and clean a real-world tabular dataset in R
  2. Identify and handle implausible or missing values disguised as valid entries
  3. Perform univariate and bivariate exploratory data analysis (EDA)
  4. Visualize relationships between features and a binary outcome
  5. Build and evaluate at least one classification model
  6. Communicate findings and limitations, including ethical considerations around health data

1.2 Dataset Description

Column Description
Pregnancies Number of times pregnant
Glucose Plasma glucose concentration (2-hr oral glucose tolerance test)
BloodPressure Diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg)
SkinThickness Triceps skinfold thickness (mm)
Insulin 2-hr serum insulin (mu U/ml)
BMI Body mass index
DiabetesPedigreeFunction Score of diabetes likelihood based on family history
Age Age in years
Outcome 0 = no diabetes, 1 = diabetes

Reflection question: Based on the summary statistics alone, do you notice anything suspicious about the minimum values of certain columns (e.g., Glucose, BloodPressure, BMI, SkinThickness, Insulin)?

3 Part 2: Data Cleaning

Several columns use 0 to represent missing data, which is not physiologically plausible (e.g., blood pressure of 0).

zero_cols <- c("Glucose", "BloodPressure", "SkinThickness", "Insulin", "BMI")

diabetes |>
  summarise(across(all_of(zero_cols), ~ sum(. == 0)))
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   Glucose BloodPressure SkinThickness Insulin   BMI
##     <int>         <int>         <int>   <int> <int>
## 1       5            35           227     374    11
# Replace implausible zeros with NA
diabetes_clean <- diabetes |>
  mutate(across(all_of(zero_cols), ~ na_if(., 0)))

# DONE: Impute missing values. Example: median imputation stratified by Outcome
diabetes_clean <- diabetes_clean |>
  group_by(Outcome) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(zero_cols), ~ ifelse(is.na(.), median(., na.rm = TRUE), .))) |>
  ungroup()

# Verify no missing values remain
colSums(is.na(diabetes_clean))
##              Pregnancies                  Glucose            BloodPressure 
##                        0                        0                        0 
##            SkinThickness                  Insulin                      BMI 
##                        0                        0                        0 
## DiabetesPedigreeFunction                      Age                  Outcome 
##                        0                        0                        0

Reflection question: Why might imputing missing values within each Outcome group separately be more appropriate than imputing across the whole dataset?

Because there may be groups that can have a value of zero in some mesures.

4.1 Univariate analysis

diabetes_clean |>

  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()

4.2 Bivariate analysis

diabetes_clean |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(Outcome)) |>
  pivot_longer(-Outcome, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Outcome, y = value, fill = Outcome)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free") +

corrplot(corr_matrix, method = "color", type = "upper", tl.cex = 0.8)

Reflection question: Does Glucose show a strong visual separation between the two outcome groups? What does this suggest about its predictive value?

We can see a little variance but we can’t make a conclusion.

4.3 Multivariate data analysis

PCA and interpretation (scores plot, loading plot and motivation de no PCs)

pca <- prcomp(diabetes_clean[,-9], scale. = T, center = T)

stnd <- pca$sdev^2

var <- (100*(stnd)/sum(stnd))

barplot(var, namq.arg = seq_along(var), col = "lightblue", main= "Distribucio de la variacio", xlab = "PC", ylab="% Variacio")

#The scree plot shows us the percentage of variance that every principal component (PC) explains. To explain enough of the variance we need at least 4 PCs to achieve 75% of the variance.

# Score plots
#PC1 vs. PC2
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2], col = as.factor(diabetes_clean$Outcome), pch=19)
text(x=pca$x[,1], y=pca$x[,2], labels= rownames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.4, pos =3)

#PC1 vs. PC3
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,3], col = as.factor(diabetes_clean$Outcome), pch=19)
text(x=pca$x[,1], y=pca$x[,3], labels= rownames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.4, pos =3)

#PC2 vs. PC3
plot(pca$x[,2], pca$x[,3], col = as.factor(diabetes_clean$Outcome), pch=19)
text(x=pca$x[,2], y=pca$x[,3], labels= rownames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.4, pos =3)

#PC1 vs. PC4
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,4], col = as.factor(diabetes_clean$Outcome), pch=19)
text(x=pca$x[,1], y=pca$x[,4], labels= rownames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.4, pos =3)

#PC3 vs. PC4
plot(pca$x[,3], pca$x[,4], col = as.factor(diabetes_clean$Outcome), pch=19)
text(x=pca$x[,3], y=pca$x[,4], labels= rownames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.4, pos =3)

#The score plots from above show us every sample distinguished of each one by their color. In the PC1 vs. PC2 we can see a tendency of the diabetics going left and the non ones to the right and the same in PC1 vs. PC3, P1 vs. PC4. But we can't see a clear separation for the others score plots.Moreover, we can't make a conclusion because in PC1 vs. PC2 we are only explaining a variance about 50%. 

#PC1 and PC2 loading plot

plot(pca$rotation[,1], pca$rotation[,2], type ="n", xlim=c(-0.5, 0), ylim=c(-0.5, 1))
arrows(x0 = 0, y0 = 0, pca$rotation[,1], pca$rotation[,2], length = 0.1, col = "blue")
text(x=pca$rotation[,1], y=pca$rotation[,2], labels= colnames(diabetes_clean[,-9]), cex = 0.6, pos =3)

5 Part 4: Feature Engineering (Optional but Recommended)

# TODO: Example — create BMI categories per WHO standards
diabetes_clean <- diabetes_clean |>
  mutate(BMI_category = case_when(
    BMI < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
    BMI < 25 ~ "Normal",
    BMI < 30 ~ "Overweight",
    TRUE ~ "Obese"
  ))

Justify why this feature might improve model performance or interpretability.

Doing this procedure, lets us know without thinking every time if a patient has high or low BMI. With this gives us another variable that gives us more information about if it is correlated.

6 Part 5: Predictive Modeling

set.seed(123)
diabetes_clean <- diabetes_clean |> mutate(Outcome = factor(Outcome, labels = c("No", "Yes")))

train_index <- createDataPartition(diabetes_clean$Outcome, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- diabetes_clean[train_index, ]
test_data <- diabetes_clean[-train_index, ]

6.1 Model 1: Logistic Regression (baseline)

log_model <- train(
  Outcome ~ . - BMI_category, # TODO: adjust formula if you engineered features
  data = train_data,
  method = "glm",
  family = "binomial",
  preProcess = c("center", "scale")
)

log_preds <- predict(log_model, test_data)
log_probs <- predict(log_model, test_data, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]

confusionMatrix(log_preds, test_data$Outcome, positive = "Yes")

6.2 Model 2: Random Forest

rf_model <- train(
  Outcome ~ . - BMI_category,
  data = train_data,
  method = "rf",
  preProcess = c("center", "scale")
)

rf_preds <- predict(rf_model, test_data)
rf_probs <- predict(rf_model, test_data, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]

6.4 ROC Curves

roc_log <- roc(test_data$Outcome, log_probs, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
roc_rf <- roc(test_data$Outcome, rf_probs, levels = c("No", "Yes"))

plot(roc_log, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curves")
lines(roc_rf, col = "red")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)

# AUC values
auc(roc_log)
## Area under the curve: 0.913
auc(roc_rf)
## Area under the curve: 0.9727

Reflection question: Compare the two models. Which performs better, and on which metric? Why might accuracy alone be misleading given the class imbalance?

The one that performs better is the randomforest according to the metric AUC (area under the ROC curve). Accuracy alone can be misleading because if one group is a lot bigger than the other, a model can achieve high accuracy by simply predicting the major group.

Reflection question: In a medical screening context, would you prioritize precision or recall for the “diabetes” class? Explain your reasoning.

We would prioritize recall, because in a medical context is best to diagnose every true positive case, prioritizing precision could lead to missing diabetic persons who need treatment, delaying this treatment and leading to more serious problems.

Write a short summary (1–2 paragraphs) explaining your findings to a non-technical audience (e.g., a clinic administrator).

We can make models of prediction for diseases like diabetes analyzing some characteristics of the subjects that we are studying. The model will be more influenced by some of this characteristics than the others and it will be more complete if we measure more characteristics and more people, also we have to control different aspects of the lives of our subjects like ethnics or environment if we want to apply the model to a certain group.

8 Part 7: Critical Reflection and Ethics

  1. This dataset only includes female patients of Pima Indian heritage. What are the limitations of generalizing a model trained on this data to other populations?

The limitations of this study are that we can’t apply the model to other ethnics or genders.

  1. The dataset is several decades old. What risks arise from deploying a model trained on old data in a modern clinical setting?

Current environmental factors and the evolution of metabolism could have changed the subjects, and so the models can be wrong.

  1. What are the potential consequences of a false negative versus a false positive in this context?

When we have a false negative the treatment could be delayed, resulting in more serious problems, and when we have false positives it could lead to additional tests or treatment that is not really necessary.

  1. What additional data or context would you want before recommending this model be used in a real healthcare decision-making pipeline?

We should ask for the ethnics, environment and location of the subjects that this model will be applied to.
